newsitem.title: USA: European rebound seen helping single currency launch.
newsitem.headline: European rebound seen helping single currency launch.

text.p: European Economic Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy forecast on Sunday better times ahead for Europe and said an increasing number of nations were likely to take part in the upcoming launch of a single currency.
"I think a significant number will be ready in 1997. When I see the present efforts I am optimistic," he told reporters.
The single currency, to be called the euro, is being launched in 1999, but countries that wish to participate must meet tough budget targets next year.

Speaking during the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, de Silguy said the improved credibility of European Monetary Union, lower long-term interest rates and a more balanced policy mix had set the stage for a rebound in economic growth in Europe.
"There are now increasing signs that a moderate recovery to a more healthy pace of expansion may be under way," he said.
De Silguy warned, though, that the expected growth would not be enough to have any visible impact on high unemployment.

He reaffirmed that the European Commission expected growth of two to 2.5 percent next year on average for the European Union as a whole. A long-awaited pick-up is needed to ensure the success of European plans for a single currency.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus also forecast a faster pace of growth in Europe next year that would help the drive to launch a single currency.
"The recent rebound in the German economy is particularly encouraging," Camdessus told the IMF's policy-making Interim Committee.
"Economic activity seems likely to be stronger in 1997... in Europe," Camdessus said. "This will help the process toward monetary unification."
De Silguy said an increasing number of European countries may be ready to meet criteria for joining EMU after a big effort to cut their budget deficits.
"Probably with more effort in the way of consolidation, I am sure there will be a significant number -- perhaps an increasing number," he added.

Italy and Spain last week unveiled budgets designed to bring their deficits to or below three percent of Gross Domestic Product next year, the crucial year for deciding which countries will join a single currency.
"Italy has made a huge effort to meet the conditions to be able to switch to the euro at the end of 1997," he said.
He said, however, there was no question of softening Maastricht Treaty standards for entry to monetary union.
De Silguy had said before the European governments announced their cost-cutting budgets this September that around seven countries would be ready for monetary union.

At a Saturday meeting of Group of Seven industrial nations, European ministers outlined agreements reached last weekend in Dublin that are designed to ensure currency and fiscal stability after the launch of the euro.
"The others are interested in the fact that when the mark disappears, its successor currency should be able to take exactly the role of the mark," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said.
"Otherwise there could be flight into the dollar which would have consequences in the currency markets. No one is interested in that happening," he said.
"They are asking questions about what the changes will mean for financial markets and currencies," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the euro would reflect the economies of the countries in monetary union -- which will include the strongest economies that have passed the test of fiscal and monetary credibility laid out in the Maastricht Treaty. "I have no wories about the (euro) exchange rate," he said.
